states.narration: You do not need to know what x and y are to see the repeated quantity. Watch what moves together when you combine the two counts.
The two copies of the expression have become one shared group. Three and two still count it; neither has been added to anything inside it.
Now change your question. Instead of asking how many wholes there are, ask what those five wholes contribute. Predict the next expression before moving on.
Every copy contained both parts, so each part receives the full count. Reverse this move to see the five contributions of each kind become five copies of the whole.

editorial.title: What counts as one thing?
editorial.setup: A whole expression can act as a single quantity. Changing what you count together can make its structure easier to see—without changing its value.
editorial.summary: The parentheses let us treat x+y as one quantity, then look inside it when that becomes useful. The step requires the same whole in both terms: 3(x+y)+2(x+z) cannot generally become 5(x+y). No division was used, so the explanation still holds when x+y is zero.
